In the 2050's, a young woman hobbyist computer programmer manages to cause an artificial lifeform to evolve using a cloud based supercomputing system that allows people to purchase a fraction of the world's combined supercomputing power on a QIPS (quadrillion instructions per second) basis.

She is approached by an entrepreneur who asks her if she can prove that a large world such the artificial lifeforms could evolve from a "Garden of Eden" configuration (ala Conway's Game of Life), even it takes a trillion years of computing time to do so, which she eventually does. She agrees to do this (even through she thinks the entrepreneur is off his rocker) in order to afford to upload her dying mother's mind up to a similar supercomputing system for a digital afterlife, which various CEO's and rich people have done first, but has slowly spread to average people. Dependent on a person's worth, they might only have one cycle of supercomputing power dedicated to their simulaton, making the outside world appear to be progressing thousands of times faster in their subjective experience. Digital people meet in a Bohemian fashion by agreeing to slow down their simulations to the speed of the poorest member.

The entrepreneur has in the meantime, uploaded several copies of himself to investigate 1) why digital copies have a tendency to commit suicide and b) if a simulated person's experience can have portions of it "skipped" and yet have that digital person's subjective experience at the time of simulation appear to not have skipped any simulation frames. One of his simulations turns out to be his biological self experiencing an uncopied simulation where he "commits" suicide, only to discover that his memory of agreeing to perform an uncopied experiment was blocked before running the simulation. By this his proves that the digital and biological experiences are identical.

As it turns out, the entrepreneur has convinced a number of wealthy investors to purchase all of the world's supercomputer time in order to launch a dual simulation, one containing the artificial lifeform's Garden of Eden configuration and another running beside it containing copies of people who want to live "forever" in a simulation that does not exist on the world's supercomputers, but in random electron configurations that have a non zero probability of spontaneously coming into existence at some point in space time.

The computer programmer finds herself waking up in "Permutation City", the portion of the simulation the has been running for 7000 subjective years. She's been awoken because the artificial lifeforms, which are now intelligent and unaware of Permutation City's existence are destroying it by developing a theory of creation that renders Permutation City's need to exist irrelevant.

After unsuccessfully trying to convince the artificial lifeforms of an existence external to their own (who have proven mathematically that their universe could have emerged out of nothingness), Permutation City escapes oblivion by developing a new Garden of Eden configuration excluding the artificial lifeforms.
